doc.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Riffs, collective ensemble and the value of a working band
summary: After an audio clip, Cullum describes alternating arranged and open passages and why six nights a week together matters.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Well let me put a — let me see if I can find this little piece right here.
It sounds great first of all.

Well you see it’s a combination. First a riff, then it goes into the collective ensemble thing. And that’s one of the things we’ve tried to make part of our style. A lot of the tunes are kind of built that way.
So you go back and forth between the little sort of arranged passage to a completely open loose passage and then back again.
And when you get to the bridge, it’s like —
When you get to the bridge and usually it becomes a solo or it becomes —
Is it hard to find musicians who are capable of that for you? You’ve had good luck.

That’s critical. I mean if we’re going to do it we’ve got to have people that can do it. So I have been able to find them and get guys to do it. One of the keys is that we’re there doing it six nights a week, over and over and over. So we’re constantly playing together. And we sort of think together, feel, it’s easier. You can take somebody that’s a stranger, you’re very sympathetic with them and you just fall into things easily with a stranger, but usually the way these things work best and it’s the advantage of an organized band.
